SEVERANCE PAY AND UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE ELIGIBILITY — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jane Doe · Acme Corp.

PURPOSE OF THIS INFORMATION SHEET
Jane Doe's employment with Acme Corp. ended on January 1, 2026. This information sheet describes, as a matter of California law, how severance pay, dismissal pay, wage-continuation payments, and payments made "in lieu of notice" can affect eligibility for California unemployment insurance benefits. This is a separate legal question from whether a claimant is disqualified under Unemployment Insurance Code § 1256 for voluntarily leaving work without good cause or being discharged for misconduct, which is addressed in a separate document in this set. A payment covered by this document can affect the weeks for which a claimant is eligible to receive benefits even where no § 1256 disqualification applies at all, and § 1256's disqualification can apply even where no severance or similar payment was ever made. This document does not determine that any payment Jane Doe received or will receive from Acme Corp. does or does not affect Jane Doe's own eligibility for benefits, and it is not itself a claim, weekly certification, or appeal filed with the EDD.

THE STATUTORY TEST: 'UNEMPLOYED' AND 'WAGES PAYABLE WITH RESPECT TO' A WEEK
California does not determine unemployment insurance eligibility for severance-type payments through a single dedicated allocation formula tied to the claimant's normal weekly wage. Instead, benefits are payable only to individuals who are "unemployed" and otherwise eligible under the code's general eligibility part, and a separate statute defines when an individual is "unemployed": among other conditions, any week during which the individual performs no services and with respect to which no wages are payable to the individual. For this definitional purpose only, the same statute defines "wages" broadly, as any and all compensation for personal services, whether performed as an employee, an independent contractor, a juror, or a witness (with a narrow carve-out for certain military duty pay not relevant here). Because a post-employment payment can be "payable with respect to" a given week even though no work is performed that week, whether a severance-type payment defeats eligibility for a particular week turns on whether that payment counts as "wages" under this definition and is payable with respect to that week — not on any statutory formula that spreads a lump sum across weeks based on the employee's ordinary weekly pay rate.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Unemployment compensation benefits are payable from the Unemployment Fund to unemployed individuals who are eligible under this part."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1251 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1251.)
  "Any week during which he or she performs no services and with respect to which no wages are payable to him or her."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(a)(1) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1252.)
  "For the purpose of this section only “wages” includes any and all compensation for personal services whether performed as an employee or as an independent contractor or as a juror or as a witness, but does not include any payment received by a member of the National Guard or reserve component of the armed forces for inactive duty training, annual training, or emergency state active duty."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1252(c) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1252.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1251 and § 1252, both directly fetched and verified twice from the California Legislative Information website using two different User-Agent strings, with byte-identical results after whitespace normalization — used as real evidence of the general statutory mechanism that determines whether a post-employment payment can affect a claimant's eligibility for a specific week. It is not a claim about which state's law governs any particular claimant's situation, and it does not determine that any specific payment received by any specific claimant is or is not payable 'with respect to' any specific week. Two of the three citations below (the § 1252(a)(1) and § 1252(c) quotations) are subdivisions of the same statutory section, § 1252, and are treated as one source rather than independent corroboration; the § 1251 citation is to a separate, independent section. Section 1252 contains additional eligibility tests not quoted here — a reduced-hours/partial-earnings test, a jury-duty/witness-service test, and an implementing-regulations provision — none of which concern severance-type payments and none of which this document addresses. How this general 'wages payable with respect to a week' test has actually been applied to severance pay, dismissal pay, wage-continuation pay, and pay in lieu of notice specifically is addressed in separate clauses below; this clause states only the general statutory test itself.

WHAT UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE CODE § 1255.3 ACTUALLY GOVERNS: THE PENSION OFFSET, NOT SEVERANCE PAY
Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3, as currently in force, does not govern severance pay, dismissal pay, wage-continuation pay, or pay in lieu of notice. Its subject is different: for any week beginning after March 31, 1980 that falls in a period during which a claimant is receiving a governmental or other pension, retirement or retired pay, annuity, or similar periodic payment based on the claimant's previous work, the statute requires the claimant's unemployment compensation benefits, extended duration benefits, and federal-state extended benefits to be reduced — though never below zero — by the amount of that pension-type payment reasonably attributable to that week. The statute goes on, in subdivisions not quoted here, to limit when this pension offset applies (among other things, to pensions maintained or contributed to by a base-period or chargeable employer, subject to further conditions) and to state that it does not apply at all if the claimant made any personal contribution to the pension or retirement plan. None of this concerns severance, dismissal, or wage-continuation pay, which are addressed in the separate clauses below.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "(a) Except as provided by subdivisions (c) and (d), the amount of unemployment compensation benefits, extended duration benefits, and federal-state extended benefits payable to an individual for any week which begins after March 31, 1980, and which begins in a period with respect to which that individual is receiving a governmental or other pension, retirement or retired pay, annuity, or any other similar periodic payment which is based on the previous work of the individual shall be reduced, but not below zero, by an amount equal to the amount of the pension, retirement or retired pay, annuity, or other payment, which is reasonably attributable to that week."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3(a) (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1255.3.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1255.3(a) — directly fetched and verified twice from the California Legislative Information website using two different User-Agent strings, with byte-identical results after whitespace normalization. This document's drafter was asked to verify, rather than assume, that § 1255.3 governs how severance, dismissal, or wage-continuation pay affects unemployment insurance eligibility. Having fetched and read the actual current statutory text directly, the honest finding is that this assumption was incorrect: § 1255.3 is, and on its face has always been since its operative 1980 date, a pension/retirement-pay offset provision, unrelated to severance or dismissal pay. This clause quotes only subdivision (a), the operative reduction rule; subdivisions (b) through (e) (the federal-conformity trigger, the two-part test limiting when the offset applies, the no-personal-contribution exception, and a retroactivity clause) are described above only in general terms and are not quoted verbatim here. This clause cites a single statutory section (§ 1255.3); no additional independent source was sought for it, since its only role in this document is to state accurately what it does and does not cover. The statutory provisions that do govern severance, dismissal, and wage-continuation pay are identified and cited in the other clauses of this document.

PAYMENTS UNDER AN EMPLOYER-WIDE OR GROUP PLAN ARE NOT TREATED AS 'WAGES'
A separate statute carves out a category of post-employment payments that are not treated as "wages" or "compensation for personal services" for unemployment insurance purposes at all, regardless of the general § 1252 wages test described above: payments to an individual under a plan or system that an employer has established for its employees generally, or for a class or group of its employees, for the purpose of supplementing unemployment compensation benefits. Benefits are not to be denied or reduced because a claimant received payments under such an arrangement or plan. On its own text, this statute is written in terms of employer-established "plans" or "systems" that supplement unemployment benefits for a class or group of employees; it does not use the words "severance" or "dismissal." How this provision has actually been read to reach group severance and dismissal pay specifically is addressed in the following clause.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Notwithstanding any other provisions of this division, payments to an individual under a plan or system established by an employer which makes provisions for his employees generally, or for a class or group of his employees, for the purpose of supplementing unemployment compensation benefits shall not be construed to be wages or compensation for personal services under this division and benefits payable under this division shall not be denied or reduced because of the receipt of payments under such arrangements or plans."
  — Cal. Unemployment Insurance Code § 1265 (California Legislative Information text), California Unemployment Insurance Code (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=UIC&sectionNum=1265.)
  Known gap: This is California statutory text — Unemployment Insurance Code § 1265 — directly fetched and verified twice from the California Legislative Information website using two different User-Agent strings, with byte-identical results after whitespace normalization. This clause cites a single statutory section; no additional independent statutory source was sought for it. The limitation disclosed in the body is a genuine one: because the statutory text itself does not mention severance or dismissal pay by name, this document does not treat § 1265's plain text alone as establishing that severance or dismissal pay is covered by it — that construction is addressed, with its own separate sourcing and its own disclosed limitations, in the next clause. This document does not address every plan or arrangement that might qualify as a § 1265 'plan or system' (for example, formal SUB-pay trust arrangements bargained into a union contract), only the specific severance/dismissal-pay application at issue here.

GROUP SEVERANCE OR DISMISSAL PAY UNDER A PLAN OR BARGAINING AGREEMENT
The California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board, in a published precedent decision, has construed § 1265 (described in the clause above) as reaching severance and dismissal pay in a specific circumstance: where the payment results from a plan or system, or from a collective bargaining agreement, and is available to a class or group of employees, the Board treats it as falling within § 1265 and therefore not as "wages" that would defeat unemployment eligibility. The Board's decision traces this construction to the California Supreme Court's 1965 decision in Powell v. California Department of Employment, which held that the Legislature's declared intent in enacting § 1265 was broad enough to reach dismissal and severance payments, and rejected an argument that whether a payment counted as "wages" should turn on the label an employer's plan documents gave it rather than on the plan's actual character.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "As we interpret the Powell case, the courts have equated severance pay or dismissal pay with the type of payments covered by section 1265 of the code. If such payments result from a plan or system or from the provisions of a collective bargaining agreement and are available to a class or group of employees, then the payments do not constitute wages."
  — Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968), California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (https://cuiab.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/precedent-decisions/pb4.pdf)
  "In essence, respondents would draw a material distinction between the supplemental unemployment benefit plans and severance or dismissal pay on the basis of the label by which the additional benefits are described in the documents which provide for the benefits. But there would appear to be no reason why collective bargaining agreements which now provide for severance or dismissal pay could not be modified to give such payments a different label and concededly qualify the discharged employee for his full unemployment insurance benefits without doing violence to the integrity of the Unemployment Insurance Fund or any party involved. To resolve the issue according to the label attached, as respondents urge, would accord greater weight to form than to substance and such a resolution is not in keeping with the obvious legislative intent expressed in section 1265 to broaden the coverage of unemployment insurance benefits."
  — Powell v. California Dept. of Employment (1965) 63 A.C. 99, as quoted in Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (Feb. 15, 1968), California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (https://cuiab.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/precedent-decisions/pb4.pdf)
  Known gap: The primary source directly fetched and verified for this clause (twice, byte-identical across two User-Agent strings) is California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (Feb. 15, 1968), a public administrative precedent decision published as a PDF on the Board's own website. Both citations below come from that same document and are not independent corroborating sources. One of the two citations reproduces language the Board itself attributes to, and quotes from, the California Supreme Court's opinion in Powell v. California Dept. of Employment (1965) 63 A.C. 99. This document's drafter attempted to independently locate and read that Powell opinion directly from a primary case-law source — Justia, FindLaw, and CourtListener were each tried — but every attempt was blocked by network access restrictions before the opinion's text could be read, and CourtListener's own search tool separately returned a daily rate-limit error. Rather than cite the Powell opinion as though it had been independently read and verified, this document sources the quoted Powell language only as it is itself quoted, verified, and reproduced within the P-B-4 precedent decision that was actually fetched and read — a genuine limitation disclosed here rather than concealed. This clause does not address how a plan's severance/dismissal-pay coverage of only some, rather than a genuine class or group, of an employer's employees would be treated, and it does not itself determine that any specific employer's severance arrangement does or does not meet this plan-or-agreement, class-or-group standard. An administrative precedent decision, as construed here, is not itself a California appellate court opinion, though the Board is bound by it and it is designated as precedential by the Board's own statutory authority.

INDIVIDUALLY CONTINUED WAGES AND PAY 'IN LIEU OF NOTICE': A DIFFERENT RESULT
The same Board precedent decision addressed a payment that did not fit the group-plan category above and reached the opposite result. There, an individual employee's employer kept him on the payroll at full salary for a period after he was told his job responsibilities had ended, paying him on the same dates and in the same amounts he would have received had he kept working, rather than as a single lump sum. The Board held these were not § 1265 severance or dismissal payments and did not fit the pattern of a normal lump-sum severance payment; instead, because each payment was tied to the specific pay period for which a normal wage payment would otherwise have been due, the Board held the payments were "wages" payable "with respect to" those specific weeks under § 1252, defeating the individual's eligibility for those weeks. Separately, the Board addressed the employer's argument that part of the payment was owed "in lieu of notice" of dismissal, and held that a payment is not meaningfully "in lieu of notice" unless the employee actually had a right to advance notice — whether by contract or by an employer custom or practice substantial enough to create an enforceable expectation of it; absent such a right, calling a payment "notice pay" does not by itself take it outside the § 1252 wages analysis either.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "The issues in this case are whether the payments made to the claimant upon termination of the employment relationship constitute "wages," and if so, to what period should the payments be allocated."
  — Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968), California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (https://cuiab.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/precedent-decisions/pb4.pdf)
  "The payments in the present case were not made in a lump sum, usable immediately in their entirety like normal severance payments. They were paid in installments at the regular wage-payment times, as though the claimant's services had been continuing."
  — Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968), California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (https://cuiab.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/precedent-decisions/pb4.pdf)
  "More important than the label, it is clear that each payment was made for the period in which services would have been furnished to earn a normal wage payment due at the time when the wage continuation payments were made."
  — Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968), California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (https://cuiab.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/precedent-decisions/pb4.pdf)
  "A necessary characteristic of payments in lieu of advance notice is that there be a right to such advance notice, or at least such a custom as would give rise to an enforceable expectancy."
  — Cal. Unemployment Ins. Appeals Bd., Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4, In re Claim of Arthur Harman (Feb. 15, 1968), California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (https://cuiab.ca.gov/wp-content/uploads/sites/13/precedent-decisions/pb4.pdf)
  Known gap: The source directly fetched and verified for this clause (twice, byte-identical across two User-Agent strings) is the same California Unemployment Insurance Appeals Board Precedent Benefit Decision No. P-B-4 (Feb. 15, 1968) cited in the clause above; all citations below come from that one document and are not independent corroborating sources of one another, though they corroborate the § 1251/§ 1252 statutory text quoted in an earlier clause of this document. This decision is now more than five decades old; this document's drafter independently re-verified, by directly fetching current statutory text, that §§ 1251, 1252, and 1265 as construed in this decision remain in force in materially the same operative terms today (see the earlier clauses of this document), but did not attempt to verify whether any more recent published decision has refined, limited, or distinguished this particular precedent's 'wage continuation' label or its in-lieu-of-notice holding, and none is cited here. This document does not determine that any specific payment any specific claimant received was, or was not, paid 'with respect to' any specific week, was or was not part of a genuine class-or-group plan, or was or was not owed under any actual notice obligation — those are fact-specific determinations the EDD, a referee, or the Board would make case by case.

Separately, the Board addressed the employer's argument that part of the payment was owed "in lieu of notice" of dismissal, and held that a payment is not meaningfully "in lieu of notice" unless the employee actually had a right to advance notice — whether by contract or by an employer custom or practice substantial enough to create an enforceable expectation of it; absent such a right, calling a payment "notice pay" does not by itself take it outside the § 1252 wages analysis either.
